full_judgment:
A. M. Mahmudur Rahman J: The Rule at the instance of the plaintiff petitioner was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the order dated 26.2.87 passed by Mr. Mohammad Mufizul Islam, Munsif, Bashkhali restoring the other suit No.78 of 1974 by his order dated 26.2.87 made in Misc. Case No. 89 of 1985 should not be set aside. 

 2. That petitioner filed other suit No. 78 of 1974 for declaration that the disputed kabala executed and registered in the name of the defendant was purchased in his benami the defendant had no title and interest therein. The defendant contested the suit and ultimately it was decreed ex-parte on 27.11.80. Thereafter the defendant filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. and the Misc. Case No. 89 of 1985 was started. The learned Munsif after hearing the case allowed it on contest holding that:- 

 The learned Advocate further argued that in absence of any application for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act the learned Munsif erred in exercising his discretion in setting aside the ex-parte decree. It is true, that no application was filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. But as the Court from examining the application and the record found that there was sufficient ground for the defendant for not appearing at the time when the suit was taken up for hearing as no notice was served upon him, the contention of the learned Advocate is misconceived. The Court can condone the delay if it finds from the application under Order 9 Rule 13 and from the record that the reasons stated in the application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. are sufficient grounds within the meaning of section 5 of Limitation Act the court can straight way allow the application and set aside the ex-parte decree. This view finds supports from the decision in the case of Mozaffer Ahmed and other -Vs- Mvi. Saleh Ahmed delivered by me reported in 40 DLR 239. This contention of the learned Advocate also fails. Mr. Karim submitted that on 27.11.1980 the suit was not fixed for ex-parte hearing. Mr. Karim placed before me today at the time of hearing the Rule a certified copy of order No. 35 dated 27.11.1980 and drawing my attention to the expression: 

 "The suit is taken up for ex-parte disposal" argued that on that date the suit was not fixed for ex-parte hearing. I am unable to accept the contention of the learned Advocate because from reading the order itself I do not find that the suit was not fixed for ex-parte hearing. The expression "The suit is taken up for ex-parte disposal" certainly means that it was taken up for "ex-parte hearing." Mr. Karim also fails to produce before me the earlier order by which the suit was fixed for hearing on 27. 11.1980. In this case it appears from the statement made in paragraph No. 16 of the petition that the learned Munsif fixed 29.1.1975 for framing issue. This shows that the defendant already filed written statement in the suit and after several adjournments on 27.11.1980 the suit was taken up for "ex-parte disposal." Where the defendant has already filed the written statement and the suit is fixed "for ex-parte disposal" it cannot be held that the court passed ex-parte decree without jurisdiction. Although it is settled principle of law that the suit cannot be heard ex-parte by the court in the event of failure by the defendant to file the written statement because the law does not debar the defendant to argue his case on the date fixed for hearing the suit in smirch as he may take the objection about jurisdiction of the court either on the ground of want of territorial jurisdiction or pecuniary jurisdiction or both and also on the ground that the plaint does not disclose any cause of action. The principle of law enuniciated in the case of M/s. Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. -Vs-The Chairman, 3rd Labour Court, Dhaka 8 B.L.D. 236 (DB), to which I was a party, only applies in a ease where no written statement was filed and the suit was decreed ex-parte on the date flexed for hearing the suit without giving the defendant' an opportunity to appear at the time of hearing the suit and to argue his case.
